summary:
Şanlıurfa is a province of Turkey and stands under the Turkish national framework. The source inventory assembled for this province contains no trans-specific material for Şanlıurfa itself: no statute, enforcement action, facility or recorded incident. A trans visitor to the province should therefore expect the national regime described here.

Turkey has no visa, entry or border rule specific to LGBTQ travellers; the documented exposure points lie inside the country. Foreigners must carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and warnings of detention for non-compliance. That requirement intersects with street-level identity checks: in August 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés in Beyoğlu, held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released them after background checks recorded under 'General Information Gathering'. Legal experts quoted by bianet argue those checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Nothing was fined in that episode, but names and details were recorded.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 on a leaked omnibus draft, the 11th Judicial Package, that would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with up to three years in prison, and to criminalise participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, surgery included, from 18 to 25, behind mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals; healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison and patients up to three years, with pretrial detention possible. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch warned it would force treatment underground and leave LGBT people in constant fear of arrest. As of that reporting the draft had not been enacted; whether it has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

Criminalisation by statute therefore had not been enacted when the package was reported, but it sits inside a broader official framing: the Erdoğan government has repeatedly used protection of "the family" and "public morals" to legitimise stigmatisation. Kaos GL's 2025 review, "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", finds that hostility toward LGBTI+ people became explicit state policy, with 'Year of the Family' instructions issued to public institutions and the closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation for the first time in years, expression and artistic freedom restricted and events cancelled or banned.

The same Kaos GL monitoring records 313 liberty violations over the year, about two and a half times the previous year, comprising 299 detention decisions (256 taken on the record, 43 off it); 89 torture and ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the prior year; private-life violations rising from 16 to 67, including obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy; 61 travel bans; and six right-to-life violations, of which three were hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected. Turkish Minute's coverage of the report counts six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected.

Hostility of this scale is documented at the level of individual cases. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy by a 17-year-old; the attacker was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, which activists describe as evidence of a state hate policy. On 1 December 2025 the transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara, and rights groups demanded an independent investigation and changes to detention practices affecting transgender prisoners. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers state that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison only two days later, and that witness statements were not taken; an opposition MP raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Detained trans visitors are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, and Turkish prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare. Some prisoners refuse hospital transfers for fear of other male inmates. No policy or staff training exists to identify LGBTI+ needs, complaints are ineffective and can provoke further violence, and transfers are frequent.

Event attendance carries its own exposure: monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Protection machinery is thin. Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no direct discrimination protection for gender identity; the European Commission's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with the EU acquis, while noting official permissions granted to demonstrations promoting exclusion. Hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately during a stay.
tangentialFactors:
The draft penal-code package belongs to a wider authoritarian drift rather than to an isolated measure, and the Erdoğan government's 'the family' and 'public morals' framing has been used repeatedly to legitimise stigmatisation of LGBT people.

Kaos GL describes 2025 as the year hostility turned into explicit state policy: 'Year of the Family' instructions to public institutions, the first closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation in years, and cancellations or bans on events. Set against that, the European Commission's 2025 report measured Turkey's legal protection for sexual orientation and gender identity against the EU accession framework and found it insufficient, while recording that official permissions were granted to some demonstrations promoting exclusion.

The August 2025 stops in Istanbul's Beyoğlu district and the resulting Article 5 European Convention on Human Rights arguments place Turkey's street-level policing within regional human-rights litigation exposure, though the cited experts frame the checks as a breach rather than a settled finding.

One detectable asymmetry in outcomes: in the August 2024 Bakırköy knifing of the trans woman Yaşam the attacker was released while the victim was referred for arrest, and in the Sincan Women's Prison death of 1 December 2025 the scene was processed only two days later with no witness statements taken. Both cases were raised by activists and an opposition MP rather than resolved by the authorities.
localsOnly:
Residents of Şanlıurfa and other Turkish provinces live under the same framework visitors encounter, but with permanent exposure: the 61 travel bans recorded by Kaos GL for 2025 restrict the movement of people living in the country, and the 299 detention decisions documented over the year fall on residents going about daily life.

Residents seeking gender-affirming care face a higher minimum age under the draft 11th Judicial Package — 25 rather than 18, with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals — and healthcare professionals who perform such interventions would be exposed to fines and up to seven years in prison, with patients facing up to three years.

Because hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, residents as well as visitors must procure and pay for it privately, and Kaos GL records obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy among the private-life violations of 2025.

Turkish citizens are also subject to the general identity-carrying requirement at checkpoints; the 3,000-lira fines attached to that requirement apply to everyone stopped, and in the August 2025 episode nothing was fined but names and details were recorded through background checks that legal experts argue breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Local organising carries documented risk: an LGBTI+ rights organisation was closed in 2025 for the first time in years, events were cancelled or banned, and expression and artistic freedom were restricted under the 'Year of the Family' instructions issued to public institutions.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 11th Judicial Package has since been enacted is unresolved in the sources; Human Rights Watch reported it as a leaked draft on 29 October 2025 and no later source in the inventory confirms its status.

No source in the inventory provides a provincial breakdown for Şanlıurfa. Whether Kaos GL's 2025 monitoring recorded any violation in Şanlıurfa specifically is not stated, and the province-level figures cannot be inferred from the national totals.

The claim that the August 2024 attacker of Yaşam was released while the victim was referred for arrest rests on activists' characterisation of a state hate policy; the inventory contains no court disposition for either party.

The Sincan Women's Prison account of delayed medical care, delayed forensic entry and absent witness statements comes from other trans prisoners, visiting lawyers and rights groups; no independent investigation outcome is available in the sources.

The European Commission's 2025 findings on insufficient legal protection are not tied in the inventory to any specific provision of Şanlıurfa's provincial administration, and no provincial anti-discrimination instrument for Şanlıurfa is sourced.

The inventory does not state whether the six deaths counted by Turkish Minute overlap fully with the six right-to-life violations in the Kaos GL report, though the two accounts describe the same 2025 reporting period.
